"""Comment-to-code boundary detector, for layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 1472.

What it does, in plain terms: this component writes into the residual stream at the
point where the text leaves a code comment and returns to code. It is near zero almost
everywhere, and fires in two places:

1. The line break that ends a comment. It is strongest (about 24) for a comment on its
   own line that starts a run of comment lines, a little weaker (about 14) for a trailing
   comment after code on the same line, and about 8 for later lines of a multi-line
   comment block. These apply to comments ending in a word, "." or "/". A comment ending in
   ")", "]" or ":" gets about 7. Empty or decorative openers ("/**", "----", triple quotes)
   get nothing, and so does a blank line after a comment (a token that is only "\\n\\n").
2. The indentation that starts the next code line after a comment line (about 6).
   A single space gets nothing.

Lines are tracked through the carry: the text of the current line, whether the previous
line was a comment, how many comment lines in a row, and whether we are inside a /* */
block. A JSON-escaped newline ("\\n", possibly split over two tokens) counts as a line
break, since code is often stored that way. Document boundaries reset the state.

What it leaves out: the diffuse noise (most positions sit near 0 with spread about 0.8), and
spikes outside comments, such as line breaks in prose. Those are not captured here.
"""
import re

READS = ()

LINE_NUMBER = re.compile(r"^\s*\d+[\t:]")  # a listing's line-number prefix, e.g. "  123\t"
COMMENT = re.compile(r"(^\s*(#\s|#[A-Za-z]|--\s|/\*)|(?<!:)//)")  # "// x", "# x", "-- x", "/*"
OWN_LINE = re.compile(r"^\s*(//|#|/\*|--)")  # the comment starts the line


def is_comment(line, in_block):
    return in_block or bool(COMMENT.search(LINE_NUMBER.sub("", line, count=1)))


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry["doc"] != doc:
        carry = {"doc": doc, "line": "", "prev": False, "run": 0, "line_block": False}
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    line, value = carry["line"], 0.0
    newline = "\n" in tok or "\\n" in tok or (line[-1:] == "\\" and tok[:1] == "n")
    if newline:
        parts = re.split(r"\\n|\n", line + tok, maxsplit=1)
        full = parts[0].rstrip()
        ends_comment = is_comment(full, carry["line_block"])
        if ends_comment and len(parts) == 2 and not parts[1]:  # the break ends the token
            end = full[-1:]
            if end.isalnum() or end in "./":
                own = OWN_LINE.match(LINE_NUMBER.sub("", full, count=1)) is not None
                value = 8.0 if carry["run"] > 0 else (24.0 if own else 14.0)
            elif end in ")]:":
                value = 7.0
        if carry["line_block"]:
            block = "*/" not in full
        else:
            block = "/*" in full and "*/" not in full.split("/*", 1)[1]
        carry.update(prev=ends_comment, run=carry["run"] + 1 if ends_comment else 0,
                     line_block=block, line="")
    else:
        if carry["prev"] and not line.strip() and tok.strip() == "" and len(tok) > 1:
            value = 6.0  # indentation opening the code line after a comment
        carry["line"] = line + tok
    return carry, value

"""Cyrillic mean shift for layer 15 MLP unit 1473.

The component reads mostly one MLP hidden unit of layer 15, unit 1473 (about two thirds
of its read direction by squared norm; the rest is spread thinly over other units). That
unit's output is silu(gate) * up. On Cyrillic tokens its up projection is strongly
positive (mean about +1.9), so its output is large and positive when the gate opens,
which happens at about 10% of Cyrillic positions. Whether the gate opens depends on
context this program cannot see, and token identity, word position and surrounding
script barely predict it. So the program predicts only the average: a slightly positive
value on Cyrillic tokens and a slightly negative value elsewhere. It explains about 0.1%
of the activation's variance.
"""

import regex

READS = ()

CYRILLIC = regex.compile(r"\p{Cyrillic}")
CYRILLIC_VALUE = 0.015
OTHER_VALUE = -0.05


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    if CYRILLIC.search(prefix.token_strings[-1]):
        return carry, CYRILLIC_VALUE
    return carry, OTHER_VALUE

"""Layer 15 MLP down-projection, rank-one component 1474 (p-82af68dd@100000).

What this program claims: almost nothing. The component's activation looks like
sign-symmetric noise with std about 0.32 at essentially every position. I could not find a
readable concept it responds to:
- token identity explains about 0% of its variance (per-token means are ~0 for every common
  token; the largest per-token means, e.g. ' but' at -0.40, cover a negligible share);
- the previous token, position in the document, and document identity explain nothing;
- whether a token repeats earlier in its document, and token class (punctuation, digits,
  function words), do not move it either;
- the one structure found is weak: neighbouring positions agree in sign 60% of the time
  (lag-1 autocorrelation 0.31), which a token-level program cannot use.
- The first token of a document is near zero (the one clear fact found).

So the program predicts 0 everywhere, the same as switching the component off. It explains
none of the activation's variance, and leaves the model's output where switching the
component off leaves it. Its harvest is empty too (CI never passes the threshold), so there
were no high-activation windows to read.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    # No readable rule was found: predict zero, i.e. the component's contribution is off.
    return carry, 0.0

"""Component layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1475: a weak, mostly unexplained feature.

What the component's activation looks like (measured on training rows):
  * Typically near zero, with a mean of about +0.03, but with heavy tails: rare
    positions reach -20 to -55 and +20 to +36.
  * Its token identity explains very little (a per-token lookup gives under 3%
    of the variance, and most of that comes from rare tokens). Its strongest
    negative values sit at clause-ending punctuation and at words that open a
    consequent ("then", "就", "なら", "please", "?"). Its strongest positive
    values sit on the word right after a wh-word or "if" ("what [it]",
    "whatever [you]").
  * Inside a sentence it is slightly negative at commas and at runs of closing
    brackets, quotes and semicolons (as in code), and mildly positive elsewhere.

This program uses only that coarse picture: clause-closing punctuation is
predicted at a small negative value, and every other token at the mean of the
rest. It does not model the rare large spikes, which depend on context that no
token rule captures.
"""

import re
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Commas, semicolons, colons, question marks, and runs of closing brackets or
# quotes, as they appear in prose and code: the clause-ending punctuation.
CLOSING_PUNCTUATION = re.compile(r"""[,，;:?)\]}'"/]+""")

CLOSING_VALUE = -0.06  # mean activation at clause-ending punctuation
OTHER_VALUE = 0.035  # mean activation at every other token


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    if token and CLOSING_PUNCTUATION.fullmatch(token):
        return carry, CLOSING_VALUE
    return carry, OTHER_VALUE

"""Layers.15 MLP down_proj, component 1476: a near-inert component.

It almost never matters: its causal importance is ~0 at every token, and switching

noise (std about 0.29) with no pattern in the token identity, token class, or
position that a short rule could capture (a per-token lookup table did not
generalise to held-out tokens). So the simplest honest program predicts the
component's typical activation everywhere: its mean, about -0.014.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = -0.0135


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # A constant prediction: no dependence on the token or its context.
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Relative pronouns: the one word class where this component reads clearly.

Component: layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1478. Its input direction is almost exactly one MLP
hidden unit (unit 1478 of layer 15), so its activation is that unit's output. The
activation is mostly small and diffuse (std 0.48), with large values on a minority of
tokens. Its largest positive values come on relative pronouns that open a relative clause
after a noun, a comma or a preposition: "people [who]", "..., [which]", "to [whom]".
Complementizer "that" after a verb ("shows that") is near 0, but this program does not
tell the two apart: every "that" gets the same value.

The program gives each relative pronoun its typical value, the word right after one a
small value, and 0 everywhere else. It is stateless: each prediction reads only the newest
word and the one before it, within the same document.

What it captures: about 1.4% of the activation's variance on eval rows (r = 0.12). A
perfect predictor restricted to relative pronouns would reach about 7%, so most of the
variance comes from diffuse context that no word list captures.
"""

READS = ()  # reads no other component

# typical activation on each relative pronoun, measured on training text
RELATIVE = {"who": 1.9, "which": 1.2, "whom": 3.0, "where": 0.8, "that": 0.4, "que": 0.5, "che": 1.3}
AFTER_RELATIVE = 0.15  # the word right after a relative pronoun is slightly positive


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    if word in RELATIVE:
        return None, RELATIVE[word]
    same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if same_doc and prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() in RELATIVE:
        return None, AFTER_RELATIVE
    return None, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP down-projection, component 1479: a weak feature that is hard to explain.

What the component is: a fixed readout of the layer-15 MLP hidden state (mostly one hidden
unit, plus many small ones). Its activation is noisy and context-driven: which token is
present explains almost nothing, and so do the neighbouring tokens. Its large negative
spikes (down to about -15) carry much of its variance, and this program does not predict them.

What this program does, in plain terms. It predicts the small, consistent tendencies we found:

  * a token that continues a word without a leading space (a later piece of a word split
    across tokens) leans negative, most of all when the word is rare: -0.32 for a rare
    English word, -0.23 mid-frequency, -0.06 common;
  * a whole word with a leading space leans negative when rare (-0.17) or mid-frequency
    (-0.09), and positive when common (+0.07);
  * a whitespace-only token leans positive (+0.14); a character split across tokens (partial
    bytes) leans positive (+0.07); punctuation, digits and other tokens sit near 0;
  * a token that already occurred earlier in the same document leans positive (+0.12), and
    more so when it recurs 4 to 63 tokens back (+0.055 more).

Word rarity is the English Zipf frequency from `wordfreq` (below 4 is rare, 4 to 5 mid,
5 and up common). On 1024 training rows the program explains about 1% of the component's
variance: it captures a little of the structure, not most of it.

Main program: `step` reads the newest token. It keeps, per document, the last position of
each token id, and resets at each document boundary, as the model does.
"""

import re
from collections.abc import Mapping

import wordfreq

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

SPACE = 0.14
PARTIAL = 0.07
OTHER = 0.01
REPEAT = 0.12
REPEAT_NEAR = 0.055  # on top of REPEAT, for a repeat 4 to 63 tokens back
# (leading space?, word rarity) -> value, for a token that is only letters
WORD = {
    (False, "rare"): -0.32,
    (False, "mid"): -0.23,
    (False, "common"): -0.06,
    (True, "rare"): -0.17,
    (True, "mid"): -0.09,
    (True, "common"): 0.07,
}


def rarity(word: str) -> str:
    zipf = wordfreq.zipf_frequency(word.lower(), "en")
    return "rare" if zipf < 4 else ("mid" if zipf < 5 else "common")


def token_value(text: str) -> float:
    if text.strip() == "":
        return SPACE
    if "�" in text:
        return PARTIAL
    if re.fullmatch(r" ?[A-Za-z]+", text):
        return WORD[(text.startswith(" "), rarity(text.strip()))]
    return OTHER


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    # carry: (document label, {token id: last position in that document}) or None
    t = prefix.position
    token = prefix.token_ids[-1]
    document = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    last = {} if carry is None or carry[0] != document else carry[1]
    value = token_value(prefix.token_strings[-1])
    if token in last:
        gap = t - last[token]
        value += REPEAT + (REPEAT_NEAR if 4 <= gap < 64 else 0.0)
    last[token] = t
    return (document, last), value

"""Predict the typical activation, but zero at the first token of each document.

The component's activation is diffuse and signed (mean about -0.06, std about 0.39)
with no concept behind it that we could find. The one regularity we saw: at the first
token of a document (position 0 after a document boundary) it is silent, close to 0.
Everywhere else it sits at its typical value, about -0.06.
"""

READS = ()

TYPICAL = -0.063


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    ids = prefix.document_ids
    first = len(ids) == 1 or ids[-1] != ids[-2]
    return carry, 0.0 if first else TYPICAL

"""Predictor for layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 1481 (a near-silent, noisy component).

What the component is: a linear read-out of MLP hidden units in layer 15. Its activation is
roughly a small signed number, mean about 0.03, std about 0.31, with no clear concept behind it.
Token identity, token category (digits, punctuation, CJK, whitespace) and running document
context explain almost none of its variance. The one regularity found is positional: each
document's first token gives exactly 0, and the next few tokens give a slightly positive value
(about 0.1), with later tokens around 0.03.

So this program predicts only that position profile: 0 at a document's first token, 0.1 for
its 2nd to 6th tokens, and 0.03 after that. It is a description of the mean, not of the
component's variance, which it does not capture.
"""

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        pos = 0  # first token of a document
    else:
        pos = carry[1] + 1
    if pos == 0:
        value = 0.0
    elif pos <= 5:
        value = 0.1
    else:
        value = 0.03
    return (doc, pos), value

What the component is: a single rank-one write into the residual stream from layer 15's MLP.
Its activation is (MLP hidden vector . V_c) * |U_c|, and that dot product is dominated by one

What this program does: it predicts the component's typical activation, a constant

MEAN_ACTIVATION = -0.013

"""Component layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1483 -- a diffuse, near-silent direction.

What it is: one rank-one piece of the MLP down projection of layer 15. Its read
direction puts about 22% of its squared weight on MLP hidden unit 1483; the rest
is spread over thousands of other hidden units. Its activation is a signed number
with mean about 0.008 and spread about 0.29.

What it responds to: no simple rule found. Hidden unit 1483 is high in some
prose contexts after words like "after", "because", "when" and low in numeric or
code checks ("exceeds", "divisible", ">=", "doesn't match"), but word lists built
from those examples explain none of the variance. Token identity, the preceding
16 tokens as a bag of words, and position in the document each explain under 2%
of it, and the component switched off barely changes the model's next-token
predictions.

So this program does not model what the component computes. It predicts the
component's typical value (about 0.008) everywhere, and 0 on the first token of
each document, where the component is always about 0.
"""

READS = ()

TYPICAL = 0.008  # mean activation over ordinary positions


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # The first token of a document (the row's first token, or the first token
    # after a document boundary inside a packed row) has activation ~0.
    first = len(prefix.document_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-2] != prefix.document_ids[-1]
    return carry, 0.0 if first else TYPICAL

"""Coordinator right after a word (weakly negative).

Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1484 writes into the residual stream
through the MLP's down projection. It is near zero at almost every position. Its clearest
behaviour is on coordinators, the words that join two items. Right after a word, an
"and", "or" or "&" goes negative, as in "safe and", "read and", "written and"; "AND" and
"&" go more negative still. A comma right after a word goes slightly negative. An "and"
after punctuation, a number or the start of a document is slightly positive.

Inside these cases the size of the activation varies a lot with context this program
cannot see, so a rule on the current and previous word explains only about 0.2% of the
variance. The program predicts the average value for each case and nothing more.
"""

READS = ()

# Average activation for each coordinator right after a word.
NEG = {"and": -0.33, "or": -0.4, "&": -0.8, "AND": -1.15, ",": -0.1}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    # The word before, if it is in the same document.
    after_word = False
    if len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        after_word = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().isalpha()
    if after_word and word in NEG:
        return carry, NEG[word]
    if word == "and":
        return carry, 0.1
    return carry, 0.0

"""Sentence-end detector for layers.15 mlp.down_proj component 1486.

This component writes into the residual stream only at the end of a sentence.
It is near 0 on ordinary words and fires on the full stop (or ? ! 。) that
closes a sentence of running text. Its response grows with how long the
sentence has been: a period after a 1-3 word fragment gives little, a period
after a sentence of about 25 tokens or more gives the full value. It is
weaker when the mark ends a line (a newline follows it), when the mark follows
a bare number ("in 1995.", "3."), and for ! and ?, and for the full-width
marks. Between sentence ends it predicts 0.

The program: at each token, if the token ends a sentence, predict the mark's
strength times a length ramp (the number of tokens since the last sentence end,
carried forward and reset at each document boundary); otherwise predict 0.
"""

import re
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# A token ending in a sentence mark, then optional closing brackets or quotes,
# then optional whitespace.
ENDING = re.compile(r'([.!?。！？])([)\]"”\'*`}]*)(\s*)$')

# Full-length response of each sentence-ending mark.
FULL = {'.': 2.8, '。': 2.8, '?': 2.2, '!': 1.5, '？': 1.2, '！': 1.2}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    new_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) < 2 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    since = 0 if carry is None or new_doc else carry  # tokens since the last sentence end
    match = ENDING.search(token)
    if match is None:
        return since + 1, 0.0
    mark, _, newline = match.groups()
    # The ramp is about 0.1 for a one-token sentence and full at 22 tokens.
    value = FULL[mark] * min(1.0, (since + 3) / 25)
    if newline:  # the mark ends a line
        value *= 0.5 if mark in '.。' else 0.0
    if len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 and prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().isdigit():
        value *= 0.3  # a bare number before the mark, as in "in 1995."
    return 0, value

"""Sorting-and-ranking detector for layer 15 MLP hidden unit 1487 (weak; mostly unexplained).

What this component is: one hidden unit of layer 15's MLP (its write is almost all of
the unit's value). Read through the unembedding, its write pushes the next-token
distribution toward "sort", "sorted", "sorting", "priority", "ranking" and
"PriorityQueue". Its activation is usually near its mean of -0.08, with occasional
large values in code and text about sorting, ordering, ranking, heaps and comparators.

The program predicts three levels, from the sorting vocabulary in the prefix:
  - 0.70 when the token being read is itself a sorting word (its mean activation there);
  - 0.07 when no sorting word is on the token but one occurred in the last 32 tokens
    of the same document (a sorting context);
  - -0.08 (the component's mean) everywhere else.
It explains only a sliver of the variance: the activation is mostly driven by context
that no word list captures.
"""
import re

READS = ()

SORTING = re.compile(r"sort|rank|priorit|heap|compar|cmp|ascend|descend", re.I)
MEAN = -0.08  # the component's mean activation
IN_CONTEXT = 0.07  # mean when a sorting word is in the last WINDOW tokens of the document
ON_WORD = 0.70  # mean when the token itself is a sorting word
WINDOW = 32


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    words = prefix.token_strings
    if SORTING.search(words[t]):
        return carry, ON_WORD
    for j in range(max(0, t - WINDOW + 1), t):
        if docs[j] == docs[t] and SORTING.search(words[j]):
            return carry, IN_CONTEXT
    return carry, MEAN

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 1488 (down_proj component 1488), as a rule-based guess.

What the unit does: its output direction promotes "(" and "()" in the next-token
distribution. It is high where an opening parenthesis is about to start a constructor
or a parenthetical, and low where a member's type has just been written after an
access modifier (public/private/...), so a method name, not "(", comes next.

What this program marks (all from the text so far, nothing later):
  - "born" (as in "Name (born 1950)"): positive.
  - a class name in constructor position, i.e. the word after an access modifier or
    at the start of a declaration, for a class declared earlier in the document
    ("class Foo" / "struct Foo"): positive.
  - a built-in or capitalised type right after an access modifier (a member's return
    or field type): negative.
  - "(" right after a capitalised word (a name, as in "Name (born ...)"): weakly positive.
Everything else is 0. The values are rough averages, not fitted per token.
"""
import re

READS = ()

ACCESS = {"public", "private", "protected", "static", "internal", "virtual", "override", "final"}
BUILTIN_TYPES = {"String", "int", "boolean", "void", "List", "double", "long", "bool", "char",
                 "float", "ArrayList", "Integer", "Object", "Map", "string"}
CLASS_DECL = re.compile(r"\b(?:class|struct|interface|enum)\s+([A-Za-z_]\w*)")
WORD_END = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z_]\w*$")
CAP_WORD_END = re.compile(r"\b[A-Z]\w*\s*$")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry["doc"] != doc:
        carry = {"doc": doc, "text": "", "classes": set(), "prev": ""}
    before = carry["text"]
    text = (before + token)[-300:]
    classes = carry["classes"] | set(CLASS_DECL.findall(text))
    prev = carry["prev"]
    stripped = token.strip()
    word = WORD_END.search(text)
    word = word.group(0) if word and re.search(r"\w$", token) else ""
    value = 0.0
    if stripped == "born":
        value = 4.0
    elif word and word in classes and (prev in ACCESS or prev in ("{", "}", ";", "::", "")):
        value = 6.0
    elif prev in ACCESS and (stripped in BUILTIN_TYPES or stripped[:1].isupper()):
        value = -4.5
    elif stripped == "(" and CAP_WORD_END.search(before):
        value = 1.0
    new = {"doc": doc, "text": text, "classes": classes, "prev": stripped or prev}
    return new, value

"""Disjunction detector: the component goes strongly negative on the word "or"
(and its equivalents in other languages) and mildly negative on other
alternative markers ("nor", "else", "rather", "alternatively", ...). It is
slightly positive on conjunctions ("and", "und", "и", "和").

The value is the component's activation on the current token only. It does not
look at context, and the program ignores everything else in the prefix.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# "or" in each language the model sees. Cased forms are matched after lowercasing.
OR_WORDS = {
    "or", "oder", "ou", "или", "eller", "vagy", "atau", "lub", "veya",
    "hoặc", "او", "أو", "或", "或者", "或是", "または", "또는", "ó",
}

# Other markers of alternatives, with the rough strength they get.
ALTERNATIVE_WORDS = {
    "nor": -1.1, "else": -0.7, "alternatively": -0.8, "rather": -0.65,
    "otherwise": -0.4, "instead": -0.3, "versus": -0.46, "vs": -0.35,
}

# Conjunctions, which the component leans slightly positive on.
CONJUNCTION_WORDS = {"and", "und", "и", "和", "et", "&&", "yet"}

OR_WITH_SPACE = -2.8  # " or": a word of its own, in running text
OR_NO_SPACE = -0.5  # "or" glued to other text (e.g. "/or", "_or"), or "Or"/"OR"
CONJUNCTION = 0.15


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    """The component's activation at the newest token."""
    raw = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    word = raw.strip().lower()
    if word in OR_WORDS:
        # CJK and other non-space scripts have no leading space, so count them as words.
        own_word = raw.startswith(" ") or not raw[:1].isascii()
        value = OR_WITH_SPACE if own_word else OR_NO_SPACE
    elif word in ALTERNATIVE_WORDS:
        value = ALTERNATIVE_WORDS[word]
    elif word in CONJUNCTION_WORDS:
        value = CONJUNCTION
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, value

"""Component layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1490 -- a "capitalized word starting a unit of text" detector.

What it does, in plain terms:
  * Its activation is strongly NEGATIVE on a capitalized word that begins a sentence,
    a bullet, or a heading (after . ! ? : a newline, or a list marker such as * - # •).
    Common function words there ("The", "In", "This", "It", "If", "We", ...) are the
    most negative, around -5.5; other capitalized words there around -4.5.
  * It is moderately NEGATIVE on a capitalized word in the middle of a sentence
    (about -2.5 for ordinary words, -3.5 for function words). That is pulled a
    little toward zero right after code syntax (=, (, ::, return, ...) and pushed
    further negative when it sits in a run of other capitalized words (Title Case).
  * It is mildly NEGATIVE (about -1.5) on a lowercase word fragment that continues
    a capitalized word (the "ness" in "Kind|ness" when split into tokens).
  * " I" (the pronoun) is about -2.
  * Everything else (lowercase words, digits, punctuation, spaces) is near 0.

Why: the component is largely a negative response to the start of a new capitalized
clause or title-like unit in running English prose. Token identity alone explains
little of the variance, so the rules use the word's capitalization, what precedes
it, and nearby capitalized words. The rules explain about a third of the variance.

The program is stateless: each prediction reads only the current and the few
preceding tokens of the prefix.
"""

import re

READS = ()

# Closed-class English words: determiners, pronouns, conjunctions, prepositions, adverbs.
FUNCTION_WORDS = set(
    """the a an this that these those it its he she they we you i in on at by for with
    from of to and or but so if because when while as then there here however therefore
    thus also not no all any some what who which how""".split()
)

# Something that ends a sentence or a line, or opens a bullet or heading.
UNIT_START = re.compile(r"([.!?:]|\n|\*|-|•|#)\s*$")

# Code syntax: brackets, operators, underscores, path separators, tabs.
CODE_SYNTAX = re.compile(r"[(){}\[\]=<>;\t_/\\]|::|->")

# A capitalized word: one capital letter then lowercase letters, e.g. "The", "Kind".
CAP_WORD = re.compile(r"[A-Z][a-z]+")


def _is_cap_word(token: str) -> bool:
    return CAP_WORD.fullmatch(token.strip()) is not None


def _capitalized_word(prefix) -> float:
    """Activation for a token that is a capitalized word."""
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2]
    is_function_word = word.lower() in FUNCTION_WORDS
    if UNIT_START.search(prev):
        return -5.0 if is_function_word else -4.5
    value = -3.5 if is_function_word else -2.5
    if CODE_SYNTAX.search(prev):
        value += 1.0  # after code syntax, less negative
    if any(_is_cap_word(t) for t in prefix.token_strings[-5:-1]):
        value -= 1.0  # inside a Title Case run
    return value


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Predict the component's activation at the newest token of `prefix`."""
    if prefix.position == 0:
        return carry, 0.0
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if token == " I":
        return carry, -2.0
    if _is_cap_word(token):
        return carry, _capitalized_word(prefix)
    # A lowercase fragment glued to the end of a capitalized piece, e.g. "ness" in "Kind|ness".
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2]
    if re.fullmatch(r"[a-z]+", token) and re.search(r"[A-Z][a-z]*$", prev):
        return carry, -1.5
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 1491, read through down_proj (component 1491).

What this component is: its input is the MLP hidden unit 1491 of layer 15
(weight 0.90 of its input direction; the rest is spread thinly), so its
activation is that unit's value times about one. It is small and noisy for most
tokens (std about 0.5), with rare large negative spikes (down to -30) inside
web boilerplate: newsletter sign-ups, copyright and disclaimer footers, and
Chinese site notices. It is mildly positive on chat-template tags such as
<think> and </think>, and it is slightly negative in the first few tokens of a
document.

What this program does: it predicts only these coarse trends from the tokens.
  - a chat or tool tag token            -> +1.0
  - boilerplate words in the last 12    -> -0.8
    tokens of the same document
  - tokens 1 to 9 of a document         -> -0.1
  - anything else                       -> 0

It explains about 1 percent of the variance: most of the activation is not
predictable from the tokens by any simple rule we found (a per-token lookup
explains about 2 percent on held-out text).
"""
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

TAGS = {"<think>", "</think>", "<tool_call>", "</tool_call>", "<tool_response>", "</tool_response>"}
BOILERPLATE = (
    "subscribe", "newsletter", "follow us", "copyright", "rights reserved", "disclaimer",
    "stay in touch", "sign up", "inbox", "headlines", "privacy policy",
    "版权", "免责声明", "关注", "本站", "责任编辑", "声明", "转载", "投稿",
)
WINDOW = 12


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    t = prefix.position
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    start = t
    while start > 0 and docs[start - 1] == docs[t]:
        start -= 1
    early = -0.1 if 0 < t - start < 10 else 0.0
    if prefix.token_strings[t].strip() in TAGS:
        return carry, 1.0
    lo = max(start, t - WINDOW)
    text = "".join(prefix.token_strings[lo : t + 1]).lower()
    if any(p in text for p in BOILERPLATE):
        return carry, -0.8
    return carry, early

Kotlin, Scala) is strongly positive, `use` (PHP) and `using` (C#) moderately, `#include` (C)

javax, android, net) is positive and the rest of the statement is slightly positive, fading
after the first segment. A Python `from x import y` line pushes it negative. Everything else
is about zero: the component's large background noise is not captured.

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

ROOTS = frozenset({"com", "org", "java", "javax", "android", "net"})

    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]

    word = tok.strip()
    value = 0.0
    if word == "import" and start:
        value = 20.0 if carry["semi"] else 3.0
        carry["seg"] = 1 if carry["semi"] else 0
    elif word == "import" and line.lstrip().startswith("from"):

class-mean predictor. It captures the strong negative spikes on fixed-pair joiners, which

- Its output direction, when its activation is negative, promotes the next-token words

  the model toward recency words: the phrasing of a text that is talking about the present
  state of things, or a span of time running up to the present.
- Its activation is strongly negative on those cue words themselves ("currently", "recently",
  "目前", "最近"), and moderately negative on words that place an event against the present or
  a deadline ("now", "until", "yet", "later", "so far", "months"), and on "to" in a span

  that no word list, token category or context bag captures; this program predicts only the

  changes the model's next-token predictions.

before it.

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Words that say "at present" or "recently": the strongest negative responses.
STRONG = {
    "currently", "recently", "目前", "最近", "現在", "现在", "今年", "今", "теперь",

"""layers.15.mlp.down_proj, unit 1503: an "algebra sign" detector with a negative
demonstrative term.

What it does, in plain terms:
1. Demonstrative determiners in running prose ("this", "these", "those", "such",
   "that") push the unit clearly negative. "this" and "these" are the strongest.
2. Arithmetic and algebra signs (+, -, =, minus sign, and also * / ^ < >) push it
   positive. The push is strongest when the signs sit in a dense stretch of maths:
   many digits, single-letter variables, brackets or other signs in the last ~16
   tokens, and most of all when the current line already contains an "="
   (for example "h(b) - h(a) = (b - a)^2").
3. Everything else is about zero.

Only the prefix is read, so it is causal. The program keeps no carry.
"""
import re

READS = ()

# Typical activation for each demonstrative (negative: they pull the unit down).
DEMONSTRATIVES = {"this": -3.6, "these": -3.6, "those": -1.8, "such": -1.8, "that": -1.0}
SIGNS = set("+-−=*/^<>≤≥≠")
# A "mathy" token: a number, a single letter (a variable), a LaTeX command, a bracket,
# or a run of sign characters; anything containing a digit or = + ^ also counts.
MATHY = re.compile(r"[0-9]+|[a-zA-Z]|\\\w+|[)(\]\[{}]+|[)(]?[+\-=^/]+|.*[0-9=+^].*")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    if tok.lower() in DEMONSTRATIVES:
        return carry, DEMONSTRATIVES[tok.lower()]
    if tok not in SIGNS:
        return carry, 0.0
    # How mathy the last 16 tokens are (0 to 1).
    recent = prefix.token_strings[-17:-1]
    density = sum(bool(MATHY.fullmatch(t.strip())) for t in recent) / max(1, len(recent))
    # Whether the current line already has an "=".
    line = "".join(prefix.token_strings[-40:-1]).split("\n")[-1]
    eq = 1.0 if "=" in line else 0.0
    value = -0.3 + 0.7 * density + 2.0 * density * eq
    if tok == "+":
        value += 1.3
    elif tok in "-−":
        value += 0.6
    elif tok == "=":
        value += 0.3
    return carry, value

clause -- "not", "no", "never", "without", "nothing", "none", "non-", "n't",

END_OF_TEXT = "<|endoftext|>"

    return token.strip().isalpha()

    counting only the same document."""
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]

  * repeat: the token's text already appeared earlier in the same document (+0.10);
  * piece:  the token continues a word, i.e. it has no leading space and is a letter
            (word-internal sub-word pieces such as "ified" in "identified") (-0.065);
  * deep:   the previous token was also a word piece, so the word has three or more
            pieces so far (-0.07 more).

A base of 0.02 is about the average activation. Coefficients are fitted by least squares
on 131k tokens from 256 training rows. On eval it explains 0.6% of the variance
(r = 0.08) and leaves the model's output almost exactly as switching the component
off does. Token identity, document language and model confidence add almost nothing
on held-out text, so this is the simplest form that keeps the signal.
The large negative spikes (down to -25) are not predicted: nothing simple here
identifies when they happen.
"""

READS = ()

BASE = 0.02
REPEAT = 0.10
PIECE = -0.065
DEEP_PIECE = -0.07


def _is_word_piece(token):
    text = token.strip()
    return bool(text) and text[0].isalpha() and not token.startswith(" ")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-2] != doc:
        carry = {"seen": set(), "piece": False}
    repeat = token in carry["seen"]
    piece = _is_word_piece(token)
    value = BASE + REPEAT * repeat + PIECE * piece + DEEP_PIECE * (piece and carry["piece"])
    carry["seen"].add(token)
    carry["piece"] = piece
    return carry, value

"""Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1527 (layer 15 MLP down_proj).

What it responds to: digits inside reference numerals. Its size is largest on the
second and later digits of a number that sits in a citation or label: "[12]" after
"[", "Fig. 12" or "FIG. 12", and "bib-0002" or "ref" tags. There its activation is
several times its size elsewhere (RMS about 8 on "[12]"-style digits against about 1
on ordinary digits). Its sign is not explained by the text: the same kind of digit
comes out positive and negative about equally often, so this program predicts only
the small average, a negative value, on those digits and 0 everywhere else.

Plain rule: a digit that follows another digit, in the same document, with a
reference marker ("[", "Fig", "FIG", "bib", "ref") among the last few tokens, gets
-1.0. Everything else gets 0.
"""

READS = ()

REFERENCE_MARKERS = ("[", "Fig", "FIG", "bib", "ref")
LOOKBACK = 12  # tokens looked back for a reference marker
PREDICTED_SIZE = -1.0  # average activation on such digits, from the sample


def is_digit(token):
    return len(token.strip()) == 1 and token.strip().isdigit()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    tokens = prefix.token_strings
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    if t == 0 or not is_digit(tokens[t]) or not is_digit(tokens[t - 1]):
        return carry, 0.0
    if docs[t - 1] != docs[t]:
        return carry, 0.0
    start = max(0, t - LOOKBACK)
    recent = [tokens[i] for i in range(start, t) if docs[i] == docs[t]]
    if any(marker in piece for piece in recent for marker in REFERENCE_MARKERS):
        return carry, PREDICTED_SIZE
    return carry, 0.0

"""Sentence-end detector for layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 1530.

The component fires on the mark that closes a sentence: a full stop, question
mark or exclamation mark that is its own token (also "。", "?", "!", and the
closing forms ")." '".' ".”" "]." "$." "!?"). On those tokens it is strong, and
its size follows the word just before the mark: a mark after a longer word
(a content word such as "process" or "information") is stronger than one after
a short word ("it", "me") or after a digit or punctuation. A mark after a single
capital letter or an all-capitals or title abbreviation ("J.", "FIG.", "Mr.")
is not a sentence end and stays at zero. Every other token predicts zero.

The program is stateless: it reads only the current token and the one before.
"""

READS = ()

END_MARKS = {".", "。", "?", "!", ").", '".', ".”", "].", "$.", "!?"}
TITLES = {"Mr", "Mrs", "Ms", "Dr", "St", "Jr", "Sr", "vs", "Fig", "Eq", "Inc", "Co", "Ltd", "Prof", "No", "Vol"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if token not in END_MARKS or len(prefix.token_strings) < 2:
        return None, 0.0
    word = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip()
    if word.isalpha():
        if len(word) == 1 or word.isupper() or word in TITLES:
            return None, 0.0
        return None, 0.9 * min(len(word), 6)
    return None, 1.0

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 1531, as the down_proj component 1531: a year-decade detector.

What it responds to: the third digit of a number in running text, the "decade" digit of
a year such as the 9 in "1939" or the 0 in "2004". Its activation is strongly negative
there, and the size depends on the first two digits: about -4.7 after "18" or "19",
-2.9 after "15", "16", "17" or "20", -0.9 after other 1x and 2x numbers, and -1.7 after
any other third digit.

Rule: if the current token is a digit, the two before it are digits in the same document,
and the one before those is not a digit, predict the value for its two-digit prefix.
Everywhere else predict 0.

The rule explains about 14% of the activation's variance on eval. What it leaves out is
mostly larger, mixed-sign values in English verse (archaic poetry with line breaks) and
on Chinese characters inside compounds, which a short rule over the prefix does not
capture.

DIGITS = set("0123456789")
DECADE_VALUE = {"18": -4.7, "19": -4.7, "15": -2.9, "16": -2.9, "17": -2.9, "20": -2.9}


def _is_digit(prefix, i):
    """Token i is a single ASCII digit in the same document as the current token."""
    return i >= 0 and prefix.document_ids[i] == prefix.document_ids[-1] and prefix.token_strings[i] in DIGITS


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = len(prefix.token_ids) - 1
    third_digit = _is_digit(prefix, t) and _is_digit(prefix, t - 1) and _is_digit(prefix, t - 2)
    if not third_digit or _is_digit(prefix, t - 3):
        return carry, 0.0
    first_two = prefix.token_strings[t - 2] + prefix.token_strings[t - 1]
    if first_two in DECADE_VALUE:
        return carry, DECADE_VALUE[first_two]
    if first_two[0] in "12":
        return carry, -0.9
    return carry, -1.7

What the component is: one direction of layer 15's MLP hidden layer. Its activation is
signed and diffuse, with no clean meaning from a single token. Most of its variance is
context it does not capture here. What the simple reading does show is:

- It is most negative on German pronouns, articles, particles and auxiliaries when they
  begin a clause: after a comma, after daß/dass/und/ist/wie, where a relative or subject
  pronoun opens a clause ("..., die", "daß er", "..., das", "aber dann").
- The same words after a preposition ("in die", "auf das") are much less negative.
- Other words are near zero, with a slight negative after a comma or a clause opener.

on 4,096 training rows of 512 tokens.

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

PRONOUNS = frozenset(
    "sich wir sie ich er es uns mich mir dich dir ihr ihm ihn ihnen welche welcher welches "
    "denen which who whom whose qui que nous".split()
)
ARTICLES = frozenset("der die das dem den des".split())
AUXILIARIES = frozenset(
    "wird werden wurde wurden ist sind war waren hat haben hatte kann können konnte soll "
    "sollen muss müssen will wollte".split()
)
PARTICLES = frozenset(
    "nun aber dann hier doch schon auch noch ja da selbst wo wenn dass daß".split()
)

)

TABLE = {
    "pronoun": {"comma": -0.61, "clause": -2.81, "preposition": -1.53, "other": -0.52},
    "article": {"comma": -2.72, "clause": -1.45, "preposition": -0.62, "other": -0.41},

def word_class(word):
    if word in PRONOUNS:
        return "pronoun"
    if word in ARTICLES:
        return "article"
    if word in AUXILIARIES:
        return "auxiliary"
    if word in PARTICLES:

"""Explanation of layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 1535 (a rank-one piece of the MLP's down projection).

What it does, in plain terms: this component is mostly a diffuse, context-dependent signal
with a small, clear structure on top of it.

1. Document start. Right after a document's first token (its second token, position 1), the
   component is strongly positive on average (about +1.4). Position 2 is weakly positive.
   The first token itself is near 0.
2. Word classes, elsewhere. Small average offsets by the kind of the current word:
   prepositions, articles and subject pronouns push it slightly negative (' at', ' As',
   ' In', ' It', ' I' and ' The' are among the most negative on average); copulas and
   negation (' be', ' was', ' not') push it slightly positive; digits, punctuation and
   everything else sit near 0.

What it does not capture: most of the variance. Within any one token or word class the
activation still varies by roughly +/-0.45 depending on context. Token identity, the previous
token, word frequency, part of speech and distance from the sentence start each explain
almost none of it on held-out text, and a linear read of the layer's residual stream explains
only about 0.3. The rule below explains about 4% of the variance on eval rows.
"""

READS = ()

DOC_START = 1.4  # mean activation at a document's second token
SECOND = 0.25  # mean activation at a document's third token
PREPOSITIONS = {"at", "in", "on", "for", "from", "with", "by", "as", "into", "about", "of"}
ARTICLES = {"a", "an", "the"}
PRONOUNS = {"i", "we", "it", "you", "he", "she", "they", "this", "that", "my", "our", "your"}
COPULAS = {"be", "was", "were", "is", "are", "been", "being", "not", "am"}
NEG = -0.13  # prepositions, articles, pronouns
POS = 0.11  # copulas and negation


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    # Where the current document started (carried from the previous position).
    start = carry if (t > 0 and docs[t] == docs[t - 1]) else t
    offset = t - start  # position within the document
    if offset == 1:
        return start, DOC_START
    if offset == 2:
        return start, SECOND
    word = prefix.token_strings[t].strip().lower()
    if word in PREPOSITIONS or word in ARTICLES or word in PRONOUNS:
        return start, NEG
    if word in COPULAS:
        return start, POS
    return start, 0.0
